utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. First of all, the Chamber would like to apologise for the late start due to the fact that one of the Judges was locked up in an area without a functioning ID and couldn't get out anymore. Before the Prosecution calls its next witness, I am informed that the Prosecution teams would like to raise a procedural matter. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Last night, there was a list of exhibits that were sent to the Chamber. There was no agreement on this recitation of these documents, this list, and I understand there is an agreement with the Prosecution that the Chamber should not examine this document until there is further review by the respective parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, pardon me. The document which was sent last night was sent in response to the Court's direction. I believe the last time was during the redirect examination of Mr. Munkelien, and it appears that the transcript at page 1697, line 1. I attempted to move these documents in across the bar table, and the Court instructed us: "If there are certain matters for which you went to present these sitreps to the Trial Chamber, please explain briefly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I see a number on my transcript which, apparently is not right. It is now 1697. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The Chamber indicated: "Please explain briefly what you are drawing our attention to and then seek it to be admitted, and then we will hear from the Defence whether there are any objections to that, so that we have a focussed view on bulky material which we receive." The document sent to you last night, or actually I sent it to Mr. Nilsson and I copied the Defence, essentially it is a spreadsheet which directs the Court's attention to the facts in each document which we believe the Court should focus on. That document was sent to the Defence over a week ago, and I asked them if they wanted to add anything to that summary, if they had a problem with the language that was used and to see if we could agree on some of the facts contained in there. As I indicated in the e-mail to Mr. Nilsson, the parties could not agree as to the content about summaries; nevertheless, I thought it was very clear that the Court wanted those summaries, and so I provided those in electronic format and intended to move them across the bar table today when I move the sitreps into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You Honour, the difficulty and the reason why these analysis are not accurate is, for example, when it is -- of course, this is tailored to the OTP's case and is not necessarily a recitation of information in here that is accurate. The difficulty comes from when there are multiple sources of information. For instance, if a soldier or officer in the ARSK provides information to an UNMO, and that's put in this document, then it is part of what the recitation is. And by looking at this document, Your Honour, you're going to get a very misleading view as to what the document is. That's why it needs additional work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I never had the impression that, by summarizing documents to two or three lines, that that could replace the document or that would be the basis on which we could work. At the same time, we often receive documents with 20, 30, 40 entries of all different kinds, and then we just do not know what the purpose of the document is. That is certainly an area which is supposed to be highlighted. I think that's what the Chamber asked for, not to get the 40 entries without knowing that the Prosecution wants to draw our attention to one, two, or three, or seven or nine. Now, therefore, if we receive such a summary - and I see them for the first time this morning, so I'm not yet contaminated - then we know at least where to look for what, and then of course we will rely upon the document. Now, apparently you, Mr. Kehoe, and I don't know to what extent the other counsel share your view, are not happy with this. Of course, if in the summary, it says, well, units X, Y, and Z, shelling intensively villages A and B, then of course we do not automatically take that for a fact. We just notice that in the report with the source mentioned, that this was reported or observed or whatever. Now, what I would like to do is, if you say it is not accurate, I don't know in -- of course, I take it that the selection made and perhaps the phrases used are OTP selections and OTP phrases which doesn't come as a surprise. Now, how are we going to resolve there problem, because what we have is a large amount of material which has relevant content, although not all of it is relevant. Therefore, my question is when the parties coming up with any other better suggestion as to how to focus the attention of the Chamber to the most relevant portions, then I'm open for that. I'm not open for lengthy litigation: On line 7, this is not correct. You know how I resolve these matters, that if you can't agree on that, then I will re-open or I will send you the schedule for the 7.00 morning meetings and the 10.00 at night meetings, where all these matters will be resolved by the parties with my assistance. How are we going resolve the matter, that is what I want to focus on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think we can resolve the matter, Your Honour. We have a week off coming up. We resolve the matter at this juncture by going through this and removing, for instance, commentary that is included in there, or how this is being presented as commentary, and then we can re-address it when we return back two weeks from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, to what extent do you need this material with the witness? I take it that in the one hour and a half you have scheduled, that you will not go through details of the all this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct. However, I would like to address Mr. Kehoe' suggestion. I did send this spreadsheet to the Defence over a week ago. I don't honestly believe that an additional week is going to produce the results that the past week has failed to produce. They were asked to review the summary I made and asked to add or comment. They didn't indicate any suggested changes, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have they expressed before today their lack of satisfaction with the way you dealt with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: They indicated by e-mail, I believe it was on Saturday and Sunday, that they simply didn't agree. I asked them specifically what didn't they agree to, and we couldn't down to the specific level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you are rather pessimistic about what could be one in the next week. Now, I see everyone standing or trying to stand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could speakers switch off their microphones after they have finished because we cannot hear the person who is actually speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We, as a Defence group, all three of accused counsel met and discussed this issue. This is the third actually summary of exhibits that we have received regarding Mr. Ermolaev, and none of the summaries are consistent or at least we've had to look at every single one. There are 78 or 79 different entries, which means that you have to look at everyone and make sure that they all much up, and I spent last night until about 10.00 with this new set that we got last night to match up to see what was consistent and what was inconsistent with the other documents that we received. Mr. Cayley sent an e-mail outlining our objections; and, obviously, we have not reached a reasonable and amicable conclusion to this. I think Mr. Kehoe's suggestion is a good one. But when we get the list of exhibits, for example, the last one that we received, the dossier had some documents that were removed, and we had to bring that up to the Prosecution's attention, and then they told us, well, some of them were removed because they were either duplicates or they were previously marked. So it is not as simple as, We gave you the documents a week or two ago, and we didn't hear anything from you. That is simply not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, life is almost more complicated than at first sight. May I be very practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Defence is willing to further specify the problems they have with these document, that we don't have to go into detail in relation to these documents with the witness. Perhaps, in cross-examination, you might touch upon certain matters. Okay. We'll then hear those specific matters, but we'll certainly not go through all of them. So to leave all those which are not specifically addressed during the examination-in-chief or during the cross-examination, to leave them for next week, when we're not sitting, you are not very optimistic, but the Defence is really excited to show to you that your pessimism is not well founded; and then if you do not agree, then I take that week off to draft my schedule for the early morning or late evening sessions, in which we will resolve the matter without any doubt. Mr. Russo, is that agreeable to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Quite understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I do have to say that I relish the early morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. You see how being locked up for a quarter of an hour strengthened my thinking about how to resolve difficult problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take that as an admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see how we can proceed. Is there any matter at that moment, Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Office of the Prosecutor calls Witness 111, Mikhail Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ermolaev. I take it you do understand the English language and you can express yourself in that language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Mr. Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ermolaev, please be seated. You will first be examined by Mr. Russo as counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, can you please state your full name for the court.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: My full name is Ermolaev, Mikhail, and father's name Mihajlovic, the full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall giving two statements to the ICTY, one dated 14th of May, 2002, and the other dated 2nd of December, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I do confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter number 4791 and 65 ter number 4792.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, looking at the screen, can you tell me if those are the two statements to which we have referred?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review those statements before coming to Court today?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is the information contained in those statements true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. The information contained in those statements are true and accurate, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do those statements accurately reflect the answers you gave to the interview questions at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Those statements accurately reflect my answers given.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you were asked those same questions here today, would your answers be the same as in those statements?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would move to mark for identification and admit 65 ter numbers 4791 and 4792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections against admission of the statements under rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The only thing I would ask is if we could get dates for 4791 and 4792 for our own reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can provided those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The 65 ter number 4791 is the statement dated 14 May 2002, and 65 ter number 4792 is the statement dated 2 December 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are the dates on which they were signed, because I see on the cover page of the first one, 25th, 26th June, 1997 and 14th of May, 2002; and on the cover page of the other, we find the 1st and 2nd of December, 2007. Madam Registrar, the first one being 4791, the 1997, 2002 statement, would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P94, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P94 is admitted into evidence, since there are no objections. 4792 the 2007 statement, Madam Registrar, would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P95, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P95 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And with the Chamber's permission, I would like to read a brief summary of the witness's 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have explained to the witness the procedure of informing the public of what is in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ermolaev is a retired captain of the 2nd rank of the Russian navy. In July of 1995, he was stationed in the UN Sector South as the Deputy Senior Military Observer. Prior to that time, he had served in two previous UN missions, including in Tuzla and Sarajevo, Bosnia, when those cities were shelled. Mr. Ermolaev became the acting Senior Military Observer for UN Sector South in late July 1995 and held that position throughout Operation Storm. He was present in Knin during the artillery attack which took place on the 4th and 5th of August, 1995, and his apartment was strung by an artillery shell while he was inside. During Operation Storm, he directed the operations of the United Nations Military Observers in Sector South. He reviewed the incoming reports from all UNMO teams in Sector South and released all of the daily and update sitreps from the UNMO teams in Sector South during Operation Storm and sent those to the UNMO HQ in Zagreb. In the weeks and months which followed Operation Storm, Mr. Ermolaev continued his role as the Deputy Senior Military Observer and made assessments of the humanitarian rights situation in Sector South based on the information reported to him by the UNMO teams in Sector South. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be very practical if the daily sitreps are annexed to P95. We will seek, in view of the matters that we discussed earlier, that they are not yet part of the admitted statement, but they will be tendered after your discussions, to receive separate numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Maybe the discussion left me behind, but I understand the issue was with regard to the summary, not to the documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I might have misunderstood that; and, of course, the summaries are not to be admitted into evidence but just the sitreps. Let's then, apart from whether it is an attachment or not, are there any objections against the admission of the sitreps as such, because if not, we'll ask Madam Registrar to prepare a list with the exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not to admission of course, but to weight, but I understand Your Honours prior rulings on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that clear. So the only remaining issue is then the summaries focussing on certain parts of these sitreps. Nevertheless, I would like to have them admitted as separate documents, which is for references far easier. Therefore, Madam Registrar, if you could prepare a list of all of the attached documents to this statement, especially the 2007 statement where they are all listed, and then provisionally assign numbers to them so that we could proceed. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, if you could please turn to your first statement, that is P94, and turn to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I apologise. May I have the assistant of the court usher. I would like to give hard copies of the statements to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems very practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ermolaev, on page 5 of P94, you discuss a meetings which you attended with General Cermak, and I'd like to you please explain the circumstances of that meeting to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Circumstances, at least as I understand it, the main purpose of the meeting was that the first meeting with General Cermak when he took over control as the person in charge for the situation in Sector South. This was the primary aim to be presented. So the delegation included our sector commander, chief of civilian affairs, and head of civilian police, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you recall the date or approximate date of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, approximate date of this meeting was maybe the -- that was the 6th or the -- 6th or the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe you have indicated a few of the people who were in attention at the meeting. Can you please tell the Court everyone you remember attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: So, initially, I got information from General Forand that we had a meeting, and the delegation included according to the agreement signed. So it included General Forand; and Civilian Affairs from Jordan, I do not remember his name; so there was another Canadian there, who I hope - this was about seven years - that was supposed to be chief UN military police sector; and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And who was in attendance from the side of the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: From the side of the Croatian authorities was the governor himself, General Cermak, with assistants and liaison officer who were in charge of providing communication with the United Nations in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And during this meeting, did the issue of freedom of movement for UN personnel, was that issue discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah. That was the primary mission of these negotiations because we clearly understood that mandate we had terminated. And so that's why, after we received from our central headquarters from Zagreb, new instructions on our activity. So that's why our first primary mission was to obtain freedom of movement and start operations, particularly of civilian police and United Nations Military Observers as it was envisioned in the agreement. So the freedom of movement was the main issue on the agenda. Initially, General Cermak stated that such freedom of movement would be given exclusively for civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do I take that to mean that he was not agreeable to freedom of movement for United Nations Military Observers?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct. He was absolutely against it. Then I just informed him to return bark to the document side between Croatian authorities and the United Nations, where it was officially stated and underlined that UNMOs as well are to conduct such a mission. Then there was a liaison officer, so his legal advisors, and they invited him to go out. They went out for several minutes and then they returned back, and General Cermak said, "Yes, okay. I allow UNMOs to have freedom of movement but only on the roads which will be given to you later."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did that limited form of movement, did that comport with your understanding of the agreement between the United Nations and the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. Because we have clear understanding from Zagreb our United Nations command, as well as, you know, we had offered a great flow of information from all conflicting sides from the United Nations and different levels, et cetera. As well, the UN Security Council strengthened the decision signed. And on the 10th of August, they decide any time, full access to any place we want to go. So that's why I do consider that such restrictions of movement officially stated by General Cermak was not in compliance with the agreement side between the government and the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And during your time in Sector South, can you tell the Court whether or not your UNMOs were ever actually given complete freedom of movement in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, you know, frankly speaking, during wartime within the Balkans, whether in Bosnia, whether in Croatia, we never experienced for United Nations structures absolutely freedom of movement. But here particularly we had strict restrictions. So, at the first stage, we were blockaded, first of all. I mean, all of our UNMOs positions, United Nations Headquarters Sector South, we couldn't even go out. So, I mean, there was no absolutely freedom of movement. So the second stage was, maybe within two weeks, the most severe restriction of movement; then gradually, more or less, due to the relations, different team leaders on their local levels, due to the decisions taken by -- on different levels as well of the United Nations and Croatia authorities. So, more or less, I can say that by September we had, let me say, relatively enough information to be able to assess situation on the ground. By the first month for sure and next, because of the restriction of movements, I assess that information collected was maybe, I don't know, 5 per cent to 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to go back now to the artillery attack on Knin on the 4th and 5th of August. Then if you could please refer to your second statement - I believe that it is P95 referring specifically to paragraph 8 - where you indicate that you were in your house in Knin on the morning of 4 August when the shelling attack again and that your house was hit by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter number 4769. Thank you. Mr. President, Your Honours, I would ask again for the assistance of the court usher. I will be asking the witness to mark two locations on this aerial photo of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you please assist the witness, but I take it after we have the map on our screen. Mr. Russo, could you first tell us whether you would need the whole of the photograph because once marking starts it is difficult to zoom in and zoom out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would probably be best if just a portion which indicates the area of the northern barracks and its surrounds could be enlarged. I believe the witness will indicate two locations in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Loading maps and photographs takes time now and then, Mr. Ermolaev, but there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, looking at this map and with the assistance of the court usher, I believe the Prosecution marks in red, if you could please circle the location of the area of your house as you recall it.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I assume it should be somewhere in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also indicate in your statement that your house was located near a school. If you could, please also -- Actually, I'm sorry, before we move to that, could you please place an "A" next to the circle you've drawn.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And please now, if you would, circle the school which you referenced in your second statement?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Should be like this, out of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And please place a "B" next to that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours, at this time, I would move for this document to be marked for identification and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see no objections. Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P96, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P96 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, the school which you have marked as "B" on that map, can you tell the Court whether or not during your time in Knin whether you saw any military use being made out of that facility by the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Personally, myself, I didn't see it; and I can say that I never seen, myself, military usage of this school by -- by the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, referring again to your second statement, this time at paragraph 13, where you discuss a document which is entitled "Provisional assessment of damage caused by HV OPs 4 to 6 August 1995 at Knin."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if we could pleas up on the screen, Exhibit P64.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, looking at document P64, is this the document to which you refer at paragraph 13 in your second statement?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document I referred in paragraph 13 of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Court when was the first time you actually saw this document?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Can you please specify your question of when did I see it? Because I wrote it, I prepared it with my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could please enlarge the "from" section and the paragraph 2, that entire part there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want you to look again at the date and the "from" line, and tell me again, if you recall, that whether or not this is the document to which you are referring in paragraph 13 of your second statement?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: This is a provisional assessment. Sorry. I just saw got your point, you know. I thought that was my summary report about the situation there. No. This document is a provisional assessment of damage caused by, yes. No, I never saw this document. The first time I just saw it and I put it down in my statement on the 2nd December when I saw it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And during your time as either the deputy or the acting Senior Military Observer for Sector South, were you ever made aware of any UNMO report concluding that the shelling damage in Knin was concentrated around military targets?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Do you mean should I comment on [indiscernible] provisional assessment that I have in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, sir. At this point, I'm only asking whether or not, during your time in Sector South when were acting as the deputy or the Senior Military Observer, if you can recall, any UNMO report at that time concluding that the shelling of Knin was concentrated only around military targets.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, pardon the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it the word "only" doesn't reflect at least to what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. The other thing I would ask is if the other microphone got turned on. His voice is fading in and out, and the microphone is off on the right side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, the report doesn't say that it was "only concentrated". It was "concentrated on," which, of course, is not related to exclusivity. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Let me rephrase the question to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, during the time as either the deputy or acting Senior Military Observer in Sector South, were ever made aware of any UNMO report concluding that the shelling damage in Knin was concentrated in the area of military targets?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And as the Deputy Senior Military Observer in Sector South, would you have expected to be informed of such a report if one had, in fact, been sent out by the UNMO HQ?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, no doubt about it, that any such an important conclusion because actually when SMO was presented, my main function then was Chief of Staff. So such a document, which is so important and sensitive, it couldn't be issued without my consideration as well and consultations, no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, just for my understanding. On the transcript, the transcribers could not hear, and neither could I, what you said, "because actually when," and then something is missing, "was presented, my main function ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I mean, that when I was in charge of Sector South, I mean alone without Colonel Steinar. So then, for sure, I just looked it throughout and released. If he was there as well himself as Chief of Staff as well, I looked through and discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I think you have indicated his first name, but can you tell the Court please, at the date that this document was sent, that is the 18 August 1995, who was the Senior Military Observer in Sector South at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: According to this paper, SMO Sector South, so it was supposed to be Norwegian Colonel Steinar, Senior Military Observer Sector South, because on that particular date, for one week, the whole headquarters and those UNMOs who spent these days during Operation Storm in headquarters, so being under stressed and et cetera. So Zagreb United Nations Headquarters asked to give situation leaves, and we all went to Zadar for several days CTO and we spent these days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want to be clear about what you just said. Are you indicating that you were not present --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- when this report was sent?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: For sure. We departed. We departed on the 17th, or something like that, and we got one week CTO. We spent them in Zadar. So I was out of headquarters. The main bulk of those were there with me, so they were out as well. So I was really surprised a bit when I saw such a paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, please, I apologise for the lack of knowledge on the abbreviations. What does CTO stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Leave days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Your Honour. I think it refers to compensatory time off.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, can please you tell the Court whether or not the Senior Military Observer Steinar Hjertnes ever mentioned to you that he believed that the shelling damage in Knin was concentrated around military targets?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No. I do not remember that we clearly discussed it and I have such clear his conclusion about what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And referring again to your second statement at paragraph 13, you indicate that you do not agree with the conclusions regarding shelling and other damage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. With regard to the leading, if we can just ask the question as opposed to the leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you're invited to refrain from leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hadn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, at the same time, of course, paragraph 13 in the second statement is in evidence. To that extent, I have not checked immediately whether the question put to the witness was in addition to what we find to paragraph 13, whether it was leading or not. But if your problem, Mr. Kehoe, would be that making reference to what we find in paragraph 13 is already leading, then my answer is that it is in evidence, and to that extent permitted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was simply making reference, as the Court suggested, to the conclusion already contained in paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I would ask, Mr. Ermolaev, if you could please focus on paragraph 2 of the provisional assessment, and explain to the Court why you disagree with the conclusions of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that it is not an official statement of the Senior Military Observer Sector South. This is internal document, and from Senior Military Observer to commander Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. What is it that you mean that it is not an official report?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I mean that we did not have, within United Nations structure, I mean UNMOs, at least for my years working with the United Nations, that I see such an unprofessional, unqualified report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicated earlier, as indicated also in the report, that it is sent to the commander of Sector South. Were the reports from the UNMOs in the HQ typically sent to the commander of Sector South or were they typically sent elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: With Sector South, I mean, you know, that all branches of the United Nations which was supposed to go over their functions, whether the United Nations civilian police, whether human rights, whether others, they have their independent chain of command. And when we cooperated and we closely cooperated with all those branches, and if there was, let me say, a request from any branch, whether from ICRC, whether from human rights, we prepared information and just give it to them. So that's why there might be a request from SMO Sector South, maybe some specific. But to me, it is absolutely -- I cannot understand, because, I mean, if such a statement, I mean, according to the procedure we have everywhere, so if you state something, then you should justify your conclusions because then it will be delegations against the same Croatian side that they allegedly shelled Knin and military objectives. This is absolutely not acceptable. If they conducted research, there must be great references, houses, analysis that close to this objective within, let me say, 50, 100 metres. There is it military objective so we know all such objectives in general on both sides. So, to me, it is not justified. It just claims that several damages, 21 damages, were observed where these damages -- well, to this document, I have more questions than answers, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving to paragraph 14 of your second statement, where you discuss an UNMO report entitled @Comprehensive survey report on humanitarian violations from HQ Sector South," from 7 August to 13 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I would ask, please, Madam Registrar, if you could pull up 65 ter number 1122.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, looking at 65 ter number 1122, do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And is that your signature which appears at the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Court what this report is based on?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Sir, this report is based on the data collected by United Nations Military Observers within the time-frame which is stated here, from 7th August to 13 September.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And looking at paragraph 1, under the main heading, "Main basic conclusions and findings," and in that paragraph, it indicates a number of figures of destroyed houses and villages searched, and there is an Annex A, which is referenced as the source of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter 4728.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, looking at 65 ter 4728, can you tell the Court whether this is the Annex A which is referenced in paragraph 1 of the comprehensive survey report?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I do confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do you recall what this document here is based on?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: So to answer this question very briefly and shortly, the report was based on daily reports we received from UNMOs, and we had some specific meeting before my departure for CTO. We gathered all team leaders in HQ Sector South. So Senior Military Observer Colonel Steinar as well was there. So I conducted the meeting, and there was a human rights team leader, this American person; and he briefed about the situation, the taskings. And together with civilian affairs, human rights, somewhere by this date we worked out such a table, and we instructed our teams, as well as just the alongside with their main mission, to start collecting information according to this table that we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And turning, again, to the comprehensive survey report, this time at paragraph 3, where it indicates the type of HRVs committed by Croatian army and police, can you please tell the Court what HRVs stand for?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Human rights violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And in that paragraph 3, there is an Annex C which is referenced as the source for the information regarding HRVs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter number 508?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, before doing so, the previous document that was on our screen, do you tender that as evidence or is it already in evidence? I saw similar lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is already in evidence, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not already, no, because this is the one which is with the signature of this witness. Now, is there any need, if the witness has identified this document, and if the parties would agree what that document apart from this signature is the P and then the number, would that be sufficient or do we have to add another 20 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had intended to move into evidence the report and both annexes as separate documents with separate P numbers; however, if the court wishes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. To the extent that the annexes are already in evidence, although not with the initials of the witness, then it produces a lot of paper. Then if anything, if we agreed that this is the document that was attached to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, these documents are not in evidence. The document which appeared at annex A is the earlier version of a document which is already in evidence. The same with Annex C, it is an earlier reiteration of a document which is already in evidence, not the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, I believe if we go back to 65 ter 4728, that's the prior exhibit, Your Honour, if we can go back to that. I do believe that that is the document that has the signature of Mr. Antilla at the bottom of it. Now, if counsel is saying it's got a the different date range, and if this is incorporated into the other document, I'm not certain if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a very practical matter. It is clear Mr. Russo says it is an earlier version of a similar document containing all kind of data. Then you're invited to sit together with Mr. Russo and see, together with him, whether there is any need to add more paper; or whether this is it another document, a previous version, and therefore allows us to compare. In that case, it makes sense --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to have it admitted into evidence. If it is the same, then, of course it does not make sense. Please proceed. Yes. You are tendering them now already or --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to at least complete establishing the foundation, if we could, again, please pull up 65 ter 508.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, looking at 65 ter number 508, is this the Annex C which is referenced as the source of information for paragraph 3 of the comprehensive survey report?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would ask that have marked for identification and admitted the survey report 65 ter number 1122, the 13 September 1995 survey which is 65 ter 4728, and the human rights violations summary which is 65 ter number 508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll go one by one. Any objection against the survey report, 65 ter 1122?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, and I see that you consult the your colleagues, Mr. Kehoe. Madam Registrar, survey report would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit number P97, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P97 is admitted into evidence. Then we come to the next one, that is the 13th of September, 1995 survey, 65 ter 4728. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just consistent with what we said before, being similar or the same document that came in under Mr. Ermolaev's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe he means Mr. Munkelien's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Munkelien's testimony. I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if you will discuss briefly during the next break with Mr. Kehoe the content and the differences of these documents, then we will hear after the break whether there is any reason to forget that number again. Madam Registrar, the 13th of September survey would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit number P98, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P98 is admitted into evidence. Then, finally, human rights violation summary, 65 ter number 508, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is similar to the document that came in, too, with Mr. Munkelien.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, also a previous version or --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I take it that you will explain to Mr. Kehoe during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is it not a previous version. What this document is that there are very time segments in the Munkelien document, and one of the time sequences is 7 August 1995 through 8 September 1995. Then, as we move through subsequent pages, it takes it on from 9 September 1995 through October and then on. So this is -- this actual document is the same exact part of a larger document that came in with Mr. Munkelien.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This particular document, insofar as it is the exact Annex C which is appended to the comprehensive survey report, it has independent significance and probative value as being that particular document, which this witness is able to identify as the source of the information upon which he made the assessments in the comprehensive survey report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say it is the same; but by being attached to this report, we better know the basis on which the report was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, is it really necessary to have additional paper into evidence which at least duplicates that? Is there any dispute about this document being attached to the report and that the witness has told us that that was on the basis of this material that the report was drafted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there is any dispute that if the witness says it was part of the report, it was part of the report. My issue is simply it is now of -- Mr. Munkelien has put this in with other things along the same title -- under the same title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, Mr. Kehoe, you're invited to present this material in such a way that the Court is fully informed about the links between and relation between the one document and the other. If the document has any new content, of course it makes sense; or if it is more limited in its content, it makes sense to have it admitted into evidence. But if it only produces more paper, then it does not make sense. We, at this moment, we will -- I'm a little hesitant, to be quite honest, where you said, Mr. Russo, that at least if I understood you well, that the content that is the text appears exactly in the same way in a document which is already admitted into evidence, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. The observations recorded do overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, for the previous document, you had the benefit of the doubt. For this document, Mr. Kehoe has the benefit of the doubt. So we will not assign a number to this document at this moment, and we will hear from you after the break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, regarding the matters reported in the comprehensive survey report which you sent, the burning and the looting and the other human rights violations to which you refer, was any of this, as far as you know, protested to any Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. So the contents, as a rule, so they were given at different levels. So, on the sector level, on the sector level, so the main source from liaison with Croatian authorities was office of General Forand. He mainly kept this relations and put down all protests of Sector South. And at least I clearly remember we discussed with him several protests which further on he put down and sent to appropriate authorities to General Cermak office, yes. There was as well, as I know, on our headquarters, Mr. Akashi, United Nations Force commander, they had their own levels of protesting this or that. But on Sector South level, yes, that was office of General Forand; and we send protests against what was reported by battalions and UNMOs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicated in your answer that these protests were sent to General Cermak's office. Can you recall or were you aware of any responses to any of these protests having been received from General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, I clearly remember one, and I think that I put it down here. That was, I think, in September, where we informed -- just before just specifying as well, sometimes protests were sent as the final resort; because in August we agreed, I mean through human rights and civilian affairs, that if we saw something I mean not good, something criminal, so we reported it to UN police and Croatian police and then they investigated it. Sometimes there was no need for such an instrument. But I remember, in September, we received with General Forand and we discussed it. We received a relatively strange, to me, a weird answer, when we strongly suggested General Cermak to stop this human rights violations and to take control, final control, of the sector. And we received a challenging answer from this gentleman which were really shocked. I was terribly sorry when I read his answer. It was stated that, allegedly, within one month in Sector South, after he took over command, no one burning of house, no one looting and anything, that everything is excellent. It was really a challenge that demonstrated to us that this person was absolutely not in the context of what was going on terrain. We immediately prepared and send him other justifications that he doesn't control the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness. I just want to be clear about the admission of the sitreps which I provided on a spreadsheet to Madam Registrar, if we could have those marked and admitted. We can certainly it that during the break or at another time when the witness is not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with it. Madam Registrar is preparing the list with the numbers; and once they're there, a decision will be given on admission. I think it would be good to have the break a bit earlier. At the same time, I have one additional question to you, Mr. Ermolaev, in relation to your last answer, and specifically on whether it is a logical conclusion that you present or that it's anything else. You said that you were really shocked by the answer, the answer saying that "no burning of houses, no one looting, and everything is excellent." You said: "That demonstrated to us that this person was absolutely not," and then what did you say, "he was not well-informed about the matters." It doesn't appear on the transcript clearly. Then that you immediately prepared and sent him other justification, "that he doesn't control the situation on the ground." Now, was this that he was not informed, because that is what I was not aware of what happened on the ground, was that your logical conclusion or were there any other reasons to establish that or to assume that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that very good specific question because you do understand that sometimes we need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, I could put the question in a more direct way. If someone says, no burning of houses, no looting, if you observed that there were burning houses and there was looting, then that leaves open various logical conclusions, one of them being that the person is not informed about what happens; another possibility is that someone does not give or does not want to admit information he has available to himself. I mean, there are several options; therefore, I am asking, is this a conclusion you have drawn; and then, of course, I would like to know why you have drawn this conclusion, rather than other conclusions, or is it in relation to other information you had that you concluded that he was not fully aware.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I got your point and I return them back to answers and conclusions. So by saying that, I meant that there is no doubt about that situation in the Sector South, General Cermak knew much better than I knew or General Forand, no doubt about it; because all main roads and all operations of Croatian police was under his direct command, and he got all information which was -- and he knew the situation there. So the conclusion here, as I mentioned, for sure, on the basis, the reports are received from UNMOs and other reliable United Nations sources cannot allow me to argue that he didn't know anything about what's going on in the area of his responsibility. So if not, so, then logical conclusion is that such an activity might be coordinated and conducted from such a level, if such an answer was given. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're telling us now is not that it demonstrated that he was not aware of what happened, but that he knew fairly well what had happened, and that you're now suggesting that it may have been orchestrated. Now, of course, again, if you're talking in terms of logic, it could be that you are aware, but you'd rather not tell that without any indicator that it was organised, but you just don't want to admit what you know. Then, again, these are two separate questions. If I do not give or if I do not reveal my knowledge of a certain situation, then, from a logical point of view, that doesn't say anything about who is responsible for the existence of that situation, and it seems that you're linking the two of them now. I'm trying really to find out what is logic, what is observation, what are the facts which were known to you, which caused you to draw these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have identified until now, say, two facts. The first one is that you were aware of reports about burning and looting, and that you had substantial knowledge of burning and looting. The other matter is that you got an answer which says no burning and looting. These are the two elements that I have at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now what else do you have for drawing any conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I a little bit just can't follow you. I am really sorry. So we just regarded, I mean, the conclusions we made about the protests and the system that existed there, and we had the facts that -- we made reports, we put facts to General Forand, and he sent protests to General Cermak, okay, and General Cermak answered that there were no looting there. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. What I'm trying to find out, in your statement, you say it demonstrated that he wasn't aware; and, therefore, you would send him information. But if I hear your testimony now, at this moment, it is that you didn't believe him that he wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, logically, yes. I mean, there are two options as you mentioned. Whether he didn't know about it, whether he knew and sanctioned it, according to my logical conclusion, as military, right, former military, and organisation of police in any country, and particularly in, well, everywhere. So I'm due confident that General Cermak knew particularly well what was going on in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're telling us now is that the answer did not demonstrate that he wasn't aware and that he did not have control, as we find in his statement; or that you rather say, no, this answer demonstrated that he was not telling us the truth and that he may well have been in control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is quite different from what we find in your statement. Therefore, I'm trying to find out whether we're talking in terms of logic and on the basis of what known facts exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is a bit, in English, in any case, it is not your native language, and sometimes you have misspelling and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, I'm suffering from the same problem with English not being my native language. At the same time, also I can imagine that if you respond in a certain way, that is to provide with information, that in the back of your mind you have the feeling that you're providing him with information not primarily because he needs that information but just to let him know that you have that information. I mean, that's the kind of logic I can understand behind such a step, especially since you tell us now that you are not convinced at all that he was not informed about the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try always to keep clear on our mind what are the facts, what are the conclusions, and if there are any conclusions on what they are based. We will have a break until 11.00, when you will be cross-examined by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, before you will be cross-examined, I will deal with a few practical matters. The parties have been provided, I take it, with a list by Madam Registrar. Have you seen that? That's the list starting with P94.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to confirm that with Mr. Russo, that is the entire dossier that was given to us; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is the last version which excised the documents which had already been admitted into evidence and the documents which are going to go in through another witness. So this represents the last spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The list I have, yes, looks like that. It is new to the extent that P numbers appear, where, of course, in any earlier versions, there could be no P numbers yet. So we see that the P94 was the first witness statement; P95 was the second witness statement; P96 was the aerial view marked by the witness; then we have P97 and P98. Now these are the two out of the three that were tendered by you, Mr. Russo. I do understand that you only insist at this moment on P97 to be admitted into evidence, and that for P 98 and the third document which was not yet marked for identification that you agreed with the Defence that there was no need to tender that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, it was my understanding that P98 was already admitted into evidence; and with respect to the another document which was 65 ter 508, we will be withdrawing that one since it is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought that you were also agreed on P98 not to be tendered, but that is apparently not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is technically a different date range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a different document, the content is not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we leave that as it is. So, P97 and P98, there is no reason to revisit P98. Then for 65 ter number 508, where I gave the benefit of the doubt to the Defence, you do not insist on tendering it anymore. So that is now off the list, it has not received a number. Then we have the other documents which are now P99 up to and including P170. These are the documents attached where there were no objections. They were already admitted into evidence but they have now received numbers, and the only remaining matter in this respect are the summaries and how to draw the attention of the Chamber to the most relevant portions of those documents. Having dealt with that, I think it is clear to everyone. Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In respect of the documents that you have just referred to, P99 to P170, I don't actually have that list, so I have the 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On this list, we see also the 65 ter numbers. If at any later stage you would find that the 65 ter numbers you had on your list do not correspond with the 65 ter numbers on this list, please inform us and then we will reconsider the admission or at least to give further possibility to argue about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you would excuse for me on a couple of occasions calling the 65 ter number, as opposed to the Prosecution Exhibit number, I will do my best to try and find them as I go through. But I think once I call that number, the exhibit number will become clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. It is not perfectly clear your last observation, Mr. Cayley. But at least as to what you said, I do not have this list. I take it, then, when working on the basis of your exhibit list with the 65 ter numbers, you will compare what we find here and see whether the 65 ter numbers you focussed on, when you did not object to admission, are the same as the ones we find here and to which P numbers are assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will do my best to locate it as I go along, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the order of cross-examination, Mr. Cayley, you're on your feet, do you remain on your feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I do remain on my feet, Mr. President, thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined, Mr. Ermolaev, by Mr. Cayley who is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ermolaev. I would like to direct your mind immediately to the matters which the Presiding Judge was asking about before the break, concerning the letter that you stated Mr. Cermak sent to General Forand in response to a letter from General Forand. You will recall that, in essence, you stated in your evidence that Mr. Cermak stated that no one is burning, no one is looting, everything is excellent. Do you recall stating that before the break?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could please call up 65 ter number 2557.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this, Mr. Ermolaev, is the letter that was sent by General Forand to Mr. Cermak. You will see, in the second paragraph, where General Forand is referring to the burning of houses and driving the poor and the destitute from their homes: "Driving poor and destitute persons, homeless from their land, in contravention of the policy of the government of Croatia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you seen this letter before?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I say that I saw a lot of paper, particularly here. So, generally, I do feel it. But to say that I particularly saw this, I cannot just remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You can't confirm you have seen the letter before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now please look at 65 ter number 4186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, do you tender this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, I do, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit number D144, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I think we have just -- yes, D 144, yes. D144 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ermolaev, here you see the response to that letter from Mr. Cermak, and I would direct you to paragraph 3 of that letter, in fact, paragraphs 2 and 3, beginning: "In the same letter, you state that ..."

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is the letter that you were referring to in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah, right, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you read paragraphs 2 and 3? I'm not going to read them out because the Judges --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Oh, yes, for sure, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, first of all, let's establish the letter doesn't say, does it, everything is excellent?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, to me, such a phrase, I ask you to give me evidence of at least one case of driving --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, I am going to interrupt you. The question I had for you is: You recall, in your evidence, that you stated that Mr. Cermak said that everything was excellent, and I need you to answer my question and state whether or not that's what the letter actually says. Does it say that, in the letter, that everything is excellent?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah, I got your question in point. You see, then, I should formulate it in a lit bit more clear way. I cannot recollect, I mean, all letters by heart. I can only relate, you know, general feelings of what was there, the substance of the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Mr. Cayley, you don't need the witness to tell us that the words, everything is excellent, appears in this letter. Your point is clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You also stated in evidence that Mr. Cermak said that no one is burning and no one is looting. Now, the letter does not say that either, does it?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Can you show me the full text of the letter, please? So here we have a statement when General Cermak was astonished at the statement of General Forand Sector South report, as you previously showed me, about persecution of the poor and the miserable from their land, which I consider are strong words and ungrounded accusations, right, in such a phrase where he claims that are there are no criminal activity against local population in such activity including all these facts that were reported by UNMOs and battalion, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in the next paragraph, General Cermak is asking for evidence, isn't he? He is asking General Forand to provide him with evidence of people being driven from their homes and their homes being burnt.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have to audibly respond, Mr. Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he states also, doesn't he, that he is ready to go with General Forand to prove the truth in any case at any time, doesn't he? That's what he states in the letter?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Absolutely, correct, that is stated in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that document, please, could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D145, marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is the next step. It is now admitted into evidence, D145. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your evidence this morning, Mr. Ermolaev, you also stated that: "Mr. Cermak had all main roads and all operations of the Croatian police under his direct command, and he got all information," and there's a gap, you pause, "and he knew the situation there." Do you recall stating that this morning?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was the chief of police in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: With all contacts between Croatian police and United Nations police, they were carried out by United Nations CIVPOL. So they were in charge of cooperating with Croatian police. I didn't cooperate. I did not recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you came to the conclusion that you offered this morning, that Mr. Cermak was in control of the Croatian police, what research did you carry out while you were serving as a military observer in Sector South to come to that particular point of view?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: So, we had different channels and institutions, I mean, in Sector South, UNMO, ICRC, human rights, civil police, and et cetera. All institutions worked according to their channels of cooperation with Croatian authorities; and through their channels of information, they presented their facts and concerns. That was done by United Nations civilian police if they found out something that was done by done by European community monitors and others. So the role of UNMOs regarding to, if I properly got it, concerning the human rights violations, that was not the proper mission I had there. You must clearly understand. So that is why we had subordinative function. And if and when we found something, we reported it to human rights --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I stop you, Mr. Ermolaev, because I want to come straight back to the question, and I'll make it more direct and more simple for you. Who told you in the Croatian police that Mr. Cermak was their commander?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, first of all, no one -- I never spoke to Croatian police myself and discussed such a question of who is in charge in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. The question is who in charge of the civilian police, the Croatian civilian police, not Sector South, so to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Right. I never discussed who was in charge of this or that structure within the governmental authority of Croatia. So the only thing that at my level I knew and reported when we met with General Cermak and General Forand, I was informed that General Cermak is in charge of general activities in the territory, for sure. I clearly understand that he had some other person in charge of different directions or activities that was organised there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But nobody expressly every told you that he was in charge of the Croatian civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The question has been asked and he answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley. Please proceed. The objection is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go back to a subject which you yourself mentioned a moment ago, and that is that you, as UNMOs, were not previously prepared for human rights monitoring. Now, I'm right in saying that, prior to the re-taking of the Knin region by the Croatian military, your job was to monitor military activity in Sector South and the zone of separation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after the 5th of August, your role changed, didn't it, to the monitoring of human rights violations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in your statement, you make it quite clear, and you can refer to it, if you wish, it's on page 2 of your statement. Let's look at it so that we're absolutely clear about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're talking about the earlier statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President, thank you. It is P94.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ermolaev - it is one, two, three, four - it's the fifth paragraph on the 1st page. Do you have that? It's your first statement. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the long paragraph, I take it, which appears on the first page after the cover page, which is numbered page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Page 2, right. No, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just so you have that in front of you, would it be fair to say that most of the UNMOs had little or no experience in the monitoring of human rights violations?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I would say yes, and I would like to just specify it a bit.
