When we discussed with General Forand on the new circumstances when our mandate actually finished, and at the same time we received, you know, agreement between Croatian authorities and the United Nations, with the new functions which are not typical for us, we write a conclusion that we need to at least get some training and understanding of what does it mean. And we organised, first of all, on commanding level, some sort of a training where ICRC, human rights, they lectured us what is the topic. I mean, it is police case, investigations, and we were never trained. So, and then before my departure for CTO to Zadar, we conducted a meeting with team leaders where we tried, I mean, at least explained what we could. And together with civil affairs and chief -- well, American human rights violations, he had 45 minutes briefing to our team leaders how it should be done, what we should report to him, and how he will react when he get such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that for much of the earlier work, at least in August, it was on the job training, really, in terms of monitoring human rights violations by UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. We clearly and vividly, so, in my position, was that the only mission of UNMO is just to, if we find out, I mean, something concerning particularly these issues, I mean, sensitive and which are in the hands or responsibility of United Nations police and human rights violations, we just immediately report it to them and then they keep on going. So a lot of information even I do not know, because we just informed them; and then it was their responsibility to conduct investigation who was killed where and et cetera. So I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to go back very briefly to your time, to your service prior to the 5th of August in monitoring the military activity, you monitored the military activity of both sides, didn't you, the Croatian military forces and also the forces of the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you had to do that, didn't you, because, as UNMOs, you needed to be impartial, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll come back to that point later. But if we could move on, and what I intend doing, Mr. Ermolaev, is to move to discrete typicals. I will tell you as we move to each one, so that you can address your mind to that particular matter. If we could now, please, talk about freedom of movement. Now I'd like you to please to turn to page 3 your first statement, that is P94, your statement taken and, I think, finally signed on the 14th of May, 2002. One question I do have for you: You started making this statement in June of 1997 and you didn't, in fact, sign it until 2002. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I can't even recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that an investigator came to see in 1997, took a proportion of the statement, and then came back nearly five years later to complete the statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if that's fair to say, but I think it's fair to say that it's speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an unclear question; that's my problem. If a statement is taken, it means that questions are put to someone, that he answers those questions, and then usually put that down on paper. What I'm interested in is whether you saw in 1997 already put on paper what your answers were during the interview that was then held; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I cannot confirm nor deny whether the text that I wrote in 1997 and 2002 are identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is where we're now talking about the text that you have written. What the Chamber has in evidence before it is a witness statement which, at least, suggests that it was the result of an interview rather than writing down a statement, because the name of an interviewer appears on the cover page, being Vyacheslav Anfinogenov, and the language that was used during the interview. But perhaps I leave it in your hands, Mr. Cayley, to find out how this statement finally found its way to paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, just to go try and go step by step, Mr. Ermolaev, and to be absolutely clear, do you recall seeing anything on paper during the first two days of the interview, 25/26 June 1997? Did you read anything on paper on that occasion. So was a typed text presented to you on the second -- at the end of the second day of the interview that you were able to read and check and correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When the -- but to be clear, it's clear from the statement that you didn't sign anything until 2002, did you? You don't recall signing anything on the 25th or the 26th of June of 1997?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you said you would take it step by step; and on the basis of one of the previous answers, I think one step is not yet dealt with. When you were interview, you said "whether my statement of 1997." Did you right a statement, or were you interviewed and did someone else put your answers on paper, or did you provide him with a written statement as guidance for questions to be put to you? Do you remember how it happened in 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't quite say for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you said you're not certain that it was the same. Let me just find that part of your answer. Yes, you say: "No. I cannot confirm nor deny whether the text that I wrote in 1997 and 2002 are identical," which suggests that at least one or perhaps even both of these statements were not put on paper by someone else on the basis of the answers you had given but, rather, that you, prepared or wrote a statement yourself. If you don't recall, please tell us, but my question arises out of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I try to, but I cannot be precise and say that I remember this with precision and what was the difference between these two cases, and why in 1997 I was first interviewed and then only I signed it, you know, five years later. I do not remember. I, as well, do not remember whether I was only orally interviewed by representatives of the Tribunal or I made -- was answering some questions in written form. Well, to my regret, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall in the second interview 14 May 2002, the second visit, whether or not you were asked any questions during that period or were you simply presented with a statement to read, correct, and sign?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I think that I just made a statement of what -- I mean, of what main feelings I had. To what extent there was some questions or not, asking me, I just do not remember. But I cannot exclude that there might be -- that some questions were asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know whether you want to explore that matter further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not at this moment. We will consider it; and at the very end, we may come back to it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, witness, if could I please direct you to page 3 of this statement, and it is in this part that you -- do you have that in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is where you set out the new duties of UNMOs, and the paragraph that I'm actually interested in is - the one, two, three - the fourth paragraph down. It's a two-sentence paragraph beginning: "Carrying out surveillance immediately in all areas." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you're talking about surveillance there, you're talking about surveillance in respect of human rights violations; yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, according to new mission we received from the United Nations headquarters Zagreb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And your understanding, at least when you made this statement, is that you would be able to carry out all surveillance, except those in which the security situation does not permit such surveillance. That was your understanding; yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of the meeting -- in fact, let me rephrase that. Did you attend the meeting between Mr. Akashi and the Croatian authorities on the 7th of August at Sector South headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where were you at that time on the 7th of August? On the 5th of August, I think you said --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: On 7th August, there is no doubt that I was at headquarters location.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you didn't attend the meeting between Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you don't know what took place at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, Your Honour, the next item that I'd like to show, actually, is a video recording of that meeting between Mr. Akashi, the special representative of the Secretary-General, and the Croatian authorities, including General Cermak. That is a meeting on the 7th of August. There is a transcript. The booths do have it. And if, please, the transcript and the video could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do that once we have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "REPORTER: 'During his visit to Knin, Yasushi Akashi spent most of the time in the UNCRO barracks where 800 civilians had taken refuge during the fighting for the liberation of the town. Here, the UN Secretary-General Special Envoy spoke to commander of the Knin garrison, General Ivan Cermak. "Following an one hour discussion conclusions which represent the implementation of the agreement with the Hrvoje Sarinic were presented. "General Cermak had given us an affirmative response regarding full respect of everything that had been agreed. Starting tomorrow, the UN and similar organisations will be able to move freely around Knin and its environs. From the day after tomorrow, freedom of movement will be extended into other areas, but this will depend on the situation in the field. "General Cermak and I agreed to call on people to stay here because they have nothing to be afraid of. Those who want to leave must be enabled to leave safely. "On behalf of the Croatian army, General Cermak has given full guarantees for all human rights and has guaranteed security to all the citizens of Knin.'" "CERMAK: 'Already today, we will talk with the people who took refuge in the UNCRO camp.'" "INTERPRETER: 'Starting from today, we shall begin speaking to, we shall begin interview the people who found refuge here in the UN compound.'" "CERMAK: 'To the women and children ...'" "INTERPRETER: 'We will speak to the women and ...'" "CERMAK. "... will be enabled freedom of movement.'" "INTERPRETER: 'Women and children will be allowed freedom of movement.'" "CERMAK: 'Return to homes ...'" "INTERPRETER: 'And return to their homes, as of now.'" "CERMAK: 'Complete social and human protection ...'" "INTERPRETER: 'They will be afforded complete welfare and humane treatment.'" "CERMAK: 'Men of military age will be enabled ...'" "INTERPRETER: '... will be given a humane and fair treatment during interviews.'" "CERMAK: 'All those who have not committed any crimes against the Republic of Croatia will go free.'" "REPORTER: 'The current conditions in the UN barracks are best known by those who have been here for two days already.'" "WOMAN: 'When our army entered, we got out and they told us not to be afraid, that nothing will happen to us, that we should go across the road where will there is a shop, and that we would be returning home. Then they said it was best if we went, I don't know where; and then they we brought us here, that it will be something for a short time only and that we are returning to our homes.'" "REPORTER: 'As we have learned from Yasushi Akashi, these people should begin leaving the barracks today in accordance withe agreement that had been reached.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to be clear -- Mr. President, to be clear about the transcript and the subtitling, you can see that what we have actually done is put in what the interpreter interpreted, and then what Mr. Cermak and Mr. Akashi actually said, and that's in brackets, and you will see that in the transcript as well. Those exhibits, the video itself, is 2D02-001, if that could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that covers the transcripts as well, Madam Registrar. D146 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If the transcript, please, could be brought up on the screen, and I just want to look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You'll see, Mr. Ermolaev, I'd like to direct attention to where it begins General Cermak. Do you see the second sentence where it begins: "Starting tomorrow." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in essence, what was said here is that the following day, on the 8th, freedom of movement would be given to the UN to move freely around Knin; and then from the day after tomorrow, the 9th of August, freedom of movement would be extended to all areas, depending on it's situation in the field. Is that your recollection of what was agreed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could now, please, very briefly, look at another video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, have we dealt with this one and also about the issue about especially the situation in the field?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm actually going to come back to it, but there is a connected video that I would like to play now which doesn't really fit in anywhere else. If, please, we could now play 2D02-0011, and this is a video from the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover]. "REPORTER: 'Mrs. Mladenka Skaric is the first of the 840 Knin civilians who took refuge five days ago in the UNCRO barracks to return home today. When we wished her all the best in the freedom of her and Croatian Knin, she told us about Milan Martic last Knin moments. "SKARIC: 'When I went down to the cellar, I found President Martic down there who was naked from waist up and barefoot, in his pants. When I saw him, I said, "Mr. President, all of the newspapers in the world should write about a president sharing the fate of his people in the cellar." At 7.15 he left us.'" "REPORTER: 'And while you are watching as cards for returning home are filled for a large number of Knin residents who will remain in Knin, let us say that this is a result of an arrangement of today between Dr. Goran Dodig, General Ivan Cermak, and Peter Pasic, government's commission for Knin.'" "DODIG: 'I have seen General Cermak for the first time today. The way in which he is trying to resolve this, his goodwill and concrete steps with which he really wants to resolve the destiny of these people, in the best possible way, fascinated me. 'And this is a guarantee, along with the principle stands of the Croatian government, Croatian leadership, and President Tudjman, that everybody has a right to a free choice and those who will remain here will have citizenship rights. 'And I think that this on-the-spot conduct like General Cermak's, I think this is the best guarantee that the situation will be resolved very soon to mutual satisfaction.'" "CERMAK: 'They will be granted as of tomorrow full protection and all civil rights in Knin, a public kitchen will be introduced with them. We have to urgently, with the help of civil authorities, which, there you are, have also from today started functioning in Knin. We, as a military structure, in all this are helping, so it goes as fast as possible.'" "REPORTER: 'For the very, a statement from Glisa Kablar of Knin and, as he himself says, a citizen of Croatia of Serb nationality.'" "KABLAR: 'I intend to stay here because this is my homeland and this is, from the liberation, my state as well. Therefore, I don't plan going anywhere else, but living here and staying here. And with these people, regardless of how they came to argue and clash, regardless of all that, I am staying here, to live and to work.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please -- I'm sorry, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If that could be marked for identification -- I'm sorry. It has been marked for identification. If it could be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D147 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, you recall the civilians that were in the UNCRO camp, don't you, during or at least prior to that time-period, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. I just recollected on particular that when this interview was taken, for sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall them also leaving the UNCRO compound around this time?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, for sure, because we live together there, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you saw in that video and it was very -- sort of went through very quickly, that Mr. Cermak was talking about opening a soup kitchen or public kitchen. Were you aware of that? I can read the transcript back to you. You're looking at me slightly puzzled.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could bring the transcript up, please, the second page. Actually, it is in your -- it's -- can you just take it down a little bit, can you scroll down, please. I think it must be over on the next page. It is where it says: "Ivan Cermak," at the very bottom. It's the text that appears under the ... yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you see there, the Ivan Cermak -- sorry, do you have that in front of you, Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah, I have, but I don't have a transcript of your comments here on the left side. Can we adjust it? No, that is the video. Can you adjust a little bit because I see myself here. Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you see that --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- the first paragraph? Were you aware of a public kitchen being opened in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I do not remember about such a direction or a reporting about the actual functioning of this structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You don't, okay. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, now, I need to present to you another UNMO report. If, please, P111 could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just to orientate you, Mr. Ermolaev, I'm going to show you an UNMO daily sitrep which was actually released by you on the 7th of August, and it concerns the matters that we have already been speaking about, and I want to show you three pages of this document. Now, you will see on the first page under highlights, do you see that? Now the highlights are the parts of the document that you as the Deputy Senior Military Observer would have drafted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, all daily sitreps are drafted by my officers. We have chief operations officer, chief military information officer, and then I am just reviewing it. So they prepare the draft; I'm just collecting or editing if there's some discrepancies, just finalise it and release it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it is not the case that you always drafted the highlights. That was often done by your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, the drafts are prepared by usually the person who is in charge, the duty officer together with the operations officer that prepare, and so partially they prepared as well highlights, if needed. I just included if I had to draw attention to something. So it was depending on the situation and depending on the analysis of the situation of the day. You know, I mean, routine work, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you read through paragraph 1. Just read it to yourself and familiarise yourself and then I have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall releasing this particular report?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you recall essentially, and I'm just going to clarify this with you, reporting that the restrictions on movement were going to be lifted the next day, on the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And slightly differently from how you characterized it in your statement about the security situation, which I don't criticize you for, but you see you say in the third paragraph, second sentence, that there will be some areas where security cannot be guaranteed. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's the paragraph 1 and then it's the third paragraph with the little dash before it. It starts: Croatian authorities stated that ...

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. I mean -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can now, please, turn to -- if I give -- is it best if I give you the ERN number to go to the next page. The ERN number begins -- the last four digits are 9577, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this, Mr. Ermolaev, to orientate you is a summary of a meeting that you had with Mr. Cermak on the 7th of August in the evening, after this meeting between Mr. Cermak and Akashi in the morning -- the meeting in the morning between Mr. Akashi and Mr. Cermak. You subsequently had a meeting with a delegation of individuals which you referred to in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is actually the next page, please. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you see at the bottom of the page, and if you could read that.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Sector South would receive information about the areas. You mean this phrase -- about security of UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If could you read from C, summary of the meetings, down to the bottom, and then let me know when you have read that and then we will go over the page.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah, I read C.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could just for completeness before I ask you any questions so that you have read the entire section --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- if we could go over to the next page, please. And if you simply read down to where it says: "Conducted on 8th August." Have you completed reading it?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I completed reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I wanted to go back to the page before to ask you some questions, but just while we're on this page were you aware at this time that one of Mr. Cermak was functions within Knin was the reestablishment of the water supply and the electricity supply? Since he mentions it in section that you have just read to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Right. So such issues as mentioned here, they were raised by General Forand and addressed to General Cermak, I mean the problems we experienced and whatever. And he was particularly in charge to carry out, I mean, water supply or some other functions so we -- I cannot say. That's why, I mean, if there was some requests they were reported to General Cermak by Mr. Forand, that's all that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify your answer, you're not aware that General Cermak was in charge of those issues, water supply and electricity supply?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I do not know, you know, hierarchy and system of governors of General Cermak, and the only thing we did so that if we had some, you know, concerns, problems and et cetera, they were reported through the channel of General Forand to General Cermak; so that's all that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So General Forand is really the best placed person to answer to the communications that took place between UNCRO Sector South and Mr. Cermak, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I stated it in written and in oral form, because exclusively it turned out particularly in Croatia that in Sector South when I arrived down there, that most communication regarding Sector South activities and liaison with Croatian authorities, as long as we had some, you know, some admin matters through our liaison team in Zadar which was responsible to ensure the cooperation between UN battalions, you know, high command as well as UNMOs with Croatian military authorities. But the system of United Nations, I mean military observers in Zadar was used as the base, as the place. So all letters of protests were sent through my team there in Zadar. They had direct contact with General Forand's office and he sent protest or information he regarded necessary to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please go back to the prior page in this document. Have I some questions for the witness on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the part that interested me, Mr. Ermolaev, is the -- you see where it say, C, summary of meetings. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw it already, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if could you please go down to the sentence that begins: "From ..." you see there that you met with Mr. Cermak for a 31-minute period on the 7th of August. You're included. You met in the former RSK headquarters with newly posted military governor of Knin, General Cermak and SKALO. Sector South delegation was told that: "UNMO, CIVPOL and other humanitarian would be able to monitor within Knin town boundaries and other areas but on 8 August afternoon would receive info about the areas where security of UNMOs and other humanitarian agencies can..." and then over the page, "cannot be guaranteed." Now is that an accurate reflection of what happened at that meeting on the 7th of August which you attended?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I already mentioned, and I want to confirm that, yes, it is absolutely exact. I mean, the feelings that I remember from this meeting and I put it down here in written form, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you didn't mention at all, did you, that General Cermak at first refused freedom of movement for the UNMOs. That is not contained in this report, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah. You see, during negotiations with conflicting parties, so we bypass several stages, so usually in the final report I put down final result, and that is the most important to me. And usually, I mean, the negotiations themselves and I do not put it down in report. We just put only facts that we received, oral promise from the government that we get, you know, everything that is stated here, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But this meeting was about the fundamental issue of freedom of movement, wasn't it? Freedom of movement for UN agencies, UNMOs, UN CIVPOL and UNCRO within Sector South. That's what it was about, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: That was about, and we received oral confirmation that General Cermak supports it. That is why I put it down into daily sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But since the issue of freedom of movement was such a fundamental issue, it seems very surprising that you didn't put down that General Cermak initially refused freedom of movement. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No. To me, I mean, I do understand that, you know, I mean, it is a little bit difficult for any person, particularly in such circumstances to take proper decision. And whenever he consulted with his, you know, legal advisors and et cetera, he turned back and articulated the correct decision that UNMOs, according to the agreement, are allowed. So to me this is the fact so that is why I didn't put it down because it is working, you know, situation and I did expect because I saw him for the first time and I just thought that everything would be as we agreed upon on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He agreed to exactly what you wanted on that day, didn't he, Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that I wanted something. So we just received an order. We changed the character of UNMOs' operations. So I had to follow the instruction that I received, so I was completely satisfied with the promises I received from General Cermak that night, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in terms of the situation on the ground at that time, you yourself mention in your statement that areas off the main roads within Sector South were often mined. Is that right? Let me rephrase the question a bit. It's not a very good question. Was there a danger of mines in the more remote areas away from main roads in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: So generally, there was such a risk, and - is it again the mic? - and such risk existed and -- yeah, this is the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And also in -- we'll come to this later on this afternoon. There was also a significant number of fighters, armed fighters from the ARSK forces within the Sector South area, who had either not fled or been captured by Croatian military forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Let me put it in such a way, in some specific areas according to information we received from Croatian colleagues, so there was such resistant -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that at that time nobody could guarantee the security of the UNMOs on the ground because of these risks, right?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I fully agree and support your statement that within the -- let me say, first several days for sure in some remote areas it was some risky operations just to go there and monitor situation, particularly if there was some terrorists or anti-terrorist activities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And when you're talking about "anti-terrorist activities" here you're referring to Croatian forces clearing the territory of enemy combatants, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I mean, those about these operations we had permanently received from General Cermak if there was supposed to be some mopping-up operations, so we received several times information about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you're a military man, that's a normal military procedure, isn't it, by any armed force to clear the terrain of former enemy combatants. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. I just confirm that in any military so, I mean, mopping-up operations in the territory is to be conducted and will be conducted; no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, what is the issue whether mopping-up operations are usual procedure? Is that in dispute or are we talking about how mopping up took place? I'm just trying to bring into my mind again what were the really issues in dispute in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think at least in some of the material that I have read, that these mopping-up operations are considered by the Prosecution as a cover for committing human rights violations and so what I wanted to establish through this witness was that these operations did take place, General Cermak did pass on information about them, and that they were perfectly proper and normal military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you have done that by that last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is good that you firmly believe in that. I mean if a mopping-up operation is considered by the Prosecution to be a cover up for human rights violations, and the question of whether mopping-up operations are usual military procedure, of course that does not give any answer to the real issue. The real issue being: What happened during these mopping-up operations? I mean, that's -- I -- I'd like the kind of questions and the kind of answers, but let's get to the core of what this case is about and you have explained it so clearly not whether mopping-up operations are normal. We're talking about how they took place. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge within those mopping-up operations specifically within your knowledge, were there any crimes that were committed that you know about personally?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we just reported all violations which took place within the course of such mopping--up operations and -- or just without officially declared mopping-up activities, because you do clearly understand that it was not a permanent procedure that all, you know, mopping up of each village and each city and et cetera, et cetera, they were reported to the United Nations, no. So only -- so in any case, we usually tried to monitor and visited such villages and if we received information that there was some -- some cases that happened during such operations, or on everyday basis, yeah, or if we saw, I mean, UNMOs saw something, so, and then that was a reporting procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But, again, can you give any specific examples of where you linked in your mind crimes that you saw with a mopping-up operation?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: We had different reports, for example, in September there was conducted mopping-up operations in some part of Sector South, and when it was started and within this course I went there myself, just to have a look what was going on, on the ground, within the framework, and on the declared so-called mopping-up operations. Well, at that particular date that I was there, so I spoke with the local Serbs. There was more than 30 or 40 in that villages, so -- and we -- they gave us information that, for example, this or that killings took place then and there, for example, this -- two houses and they were just killed and buried in front of the doors, et cetera. So my responsibility was that I received as unconfirmed information from locals to human rights and, you know, just to confirm or disconfirm whether they were killed or not, I do not know. Then another example, for example, on the main road, UNMOs, on 23rd August, found two bodies of dead Serbs. So we reported to civil police and Croatian authorities so that there are two bodies along the main road, so please take them away. And after a week in September, I sent a car there to check whether these bodies were taken away, but they were only moved there and covered with a blanket and the head was thrown in the house [sic]. So I mean, sometimes, you know, it is not the case, if you want other examples. So I mean now we just -- during such operations mostly what we could see when we entered the zone, when and if we are authorised, we could see burned houses, we could see killed livestock or we could see that this livestock was transported to south in the south direction in the special vehicles. That's the consequences of mopping-up operations. Frankly speaking, I never received and never saw and we didn't discuss it, I mean, what are the main results, what are the main outcomes, how many people were found, what happened to them, how many prisoners of war. We never received updates or just answers or no detailed reports, so that's why I -- that's -- the main conclusion then is that after we checked mopping-up areas, we found dead bodies, blasted houses, blood, and if there was some people left, they described, you know, the situation that happened. We cannot confirm or deny what they told us, but, I mean, we just relay this information to human rights and civilian police because that is not function of UNMO to, you know, investigate what really happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were not able to specifically link the mopping-up operation with the crimes that you saw on the ground. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I believe the witness's last answer covered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The whole issue we're dealing with is a bit of a different one. Are mopping-up operations normal, acceptable procedure. What exactly -- and that of course appears to be the issue: What is a mopping-up operation? Let me just give it a try, Mr. Ermolaev. Is a mopping-up operation an operation in which you clear the terrain from military presence after intense combat activities have taken place? Would that be a definition more or less of a -- of a mopping-up operation? Because you're talking about mopping-up operations --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think that more correct may be -- there must be another for sure terminology. Maybe, I don't know, so I need some time just in English language. Maybe later on I try to -- it's a little bit another definition because mopping it's like cleansing, you know. And mopping, when you've taken control of the ground that means, at least as we military understand it. So if there, let me say, some enemy soldiers left there and you take control over the situation so -- and I do not think that, well, a little bit proper English for it. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if now, for approximately five to ten minutes, questions have been put to you in relation to mopping-up operations without explanation on what is exactly understood by mopping-up operation. And where you have difficulties to define it, then that exactly demonstrates the concern I earlier expressed what we're actually talking about. Mr. Cayley, if you want to put any further questions in relation to mopping-up operations you should first explain to the witness what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had some specific questions. I mean, I opened it up because that's what I understood from you that you wanted me to do. But this issue I'm going to address it later with a specific example that the witness refers to in his statement so I can come back to it at that point. And in fact I can go back to the point that we were discussing before this whole freedom of movement. But I notice that the time is running towards the break, so I can either start that now or wait until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want you to know that if you have not defined what a certain type of operation is and if the witness says he doesn't know exactly in the English language how to define it, that the probative value of whatever comes out of such an examination is limited, very limited. The Chamber always has insisted on the best productivity available. I'm not going to tell you or to have a debate exactly on put this question or put that question or deal with this matter. I just wanted you -- to explain what my concern was. Your reference to the break was a good one. We'll first ask the usher to escort Mr. Ermolaev out of the courtroom. We have a break for approximately 20 minutes, Mr. Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the clock to know when the break is one way of looking at the clock. I look at the clock in a bit of a different way; that is, how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that I will probably require the rest of the session and some more time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's as vague an answer as I would have given if I were in your position. Yes, some more time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm going to make another excuse and consult with lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Then I'll hear meanwhile from other counsel what they think they would need. Mr. Kuzmanovic, meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We've decided the order. I'm going to be going second and I will take approximately an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately an hour. Mr. Kehoe, you will be third then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge. I have a couple of questions. As I probably -- depending on my colleague Mr. Cayley, I don't really know all the areas he is going to cover. Certainly we're not going overlap but I'm certainly not going to re-tread or go over that again which he goes over. But I can't -- I would think an hour and a half, two hours at the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will consider it. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow the first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would bring us then -- it would take a little less than the whole of the morning session. Let's just see, the first session. Mr. Cayley asks for that. Then Mr. Kuzmanovic you said one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately an hour, give or take, 15 minutes either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you, one half to two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd say definitely two hours, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two hours. Brings us to ... so you would be through tomorrow's session, which is effectively only four hours. We will consider it. We'll have a break and resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has briefly considered timing, and we'll come up with some further details later, but the Chamber is, at this moment, takes the view that the examination of this witness could be finished by tomorrow. That will mean that some time should remain for Mr. Russo, for questions by the Bench. If we provisionally assess the time needed for that at 45 minutes, that would mean that tomorrow for Defence there would be approximately three hours left. That's what the Chamber takes as a starting point at this moment, and of course, always, views on these matters are provisional, because you never know what happens during the cross-examination or further examination. But this is what the Chamber has in mind, in view of the way it went until now. Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could please have P114 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, just to orientate you, this is an UNMO daily sitrep from the 10th of August. It was actually released by Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes, not by yourself. And what interests me on this particular document is the second page, which is 9588, and paragraph 1 under B, ground activity. Now, you saw the date of the document, Mr. Ermolaev, is 10th of August, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this in fact demonstrates that by the 10th of August, the headquarters patrol of UNMO, the UNMO Sector South patrol was in fact patrolling the region, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now if we could, please, go to page 9590. And the paragraph that interests me here is the first paragraph. If you could just read that through. Have you read that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: First of all, do you recall that event taking place on the 10th of August, that the headquarters patrol was stopped at Benkovac by the police?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, it's -- I want to say that I cannot remember, I'm sorry, on each case, each statement today what happened particularly at that time at Benkovac or any other area. So, but if it is stated there, that means that it happened, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now in your statement at page 6, and this is P94 that I'm now referring to. Do you have your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Oh yes. Page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I advise the person to choose a better ring tone, but apart from that, mobile phones ringing in court are usually seized and -- yes. Well, it seems that a need for the telephone conversation has diminished. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, sorry about that. It is your first statement, page 6. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what interests me is the first paragraph and the last sentence within that paragraph and it begins after the word -- General Gotovina's name is misspelled there. You will see that it says: "It should be outlined that even on the authorised by Cermak roads very often UN military observers were stopped at the Croatian check-points and were not allowed to proceed with the carrying out of their functions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you recall that as being a fact, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you one last document on this particular subject and then I will have a series of questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the -- one moment, Mr. President. Thank you. Could I please have 65 ter 1194, please, brought up on the screen. And if this, please, Mr. President, could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D148 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go over the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You see on the first page there it is speaking about the restriction of freedom of movement, Mr. Ermolaev. Do you see that, paragraph B?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it's talking about the various sectors. And then if we go to -- over the page it speaks about Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yeah. If you read that second paragraph where it says "SS," standing for Sector South. Have you read that? It's the second full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: "This week UN CIVPOL ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was that your experience on the ground, that on occasions local commanders of police or HV units essentially restricted freedom of movement in a particular area?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. We received different information from different teams, at least as I recollect it, that there were different reasons mentioned, and I do believe that in general, so usually they met some, well, check-points or where they were bypassing and they were stopped with the different [indiscernible] or whatever and they were prevented with proceeding with their functions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And those local commanders were acting at variance with what had been agreed on freedom of movement at a higher level, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Can we just rephrase, please. At variance, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Those local commanders who were restricting freedom of movement were not acting in accordance with what had been agreed on freedom of movement between the Croatian authorities and the United Nations. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. We do consider, you know, that - I'm just speaking about not CIVPOL, it is a bit not my area - that UNMOs didn't get full freedom of movement at any time and without explanations what they're doing here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm not -- you're last response is a little unclear to me. The question that I had for you was, was it your experience on the ground as UNMOs, and I don't have an UNMO document that reflects this is why I'm showing you a UN CIVPOL document, you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No, no, but generally it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is expressed in that paragraph about, you know, this -- the discretion of HV police commanders exercising their discretion on freedom of movement, was that your experience, what's reflected there?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If please the witness could be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, this document, page 1 and page 4 apparently has markings on it which in copying the document give the effect of a redaction. The Chamber cannot read the whole of the document, bottom of the first page, page 4 as well. Is there any possibility that you upload a copy which does not have this disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution document, so I can certainly consult with Mr. Russo or Mr. Tieger about having a document without redactions uploaded into the system, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, I take it you're ready to assist Mr. Cayley in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Always, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could have D92.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Ermolaev, not a document that you released as the Deputy Senior Military Observer, but one, nevertheless, that I would like to ask you a few questions about. Now in paragraph 1, you'll see in the second sentence: "All check-points in the area of Knin are now manned by the Croatian police." And the date of that report is the 18th of August, 1995. Do you recall that taking place, that all check-points were occupied by the civilian police in the area of Knin by the 18th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah, a very good question. So at least as I remember and recollect, as soon as General Cermak arrived and took over command over the sector, so of this terrain, territory, so I do feel myself that he took over control and check-points from military not later than maybe three or four days after the end of OP Storm. So I think that in Knin area that was maybe not later than 10th of August. I cannot recollect it exactly, but -- well, my understanding and my feelings that as soon as he arrived in Knin and around Knin, so there were check-points and everything, they were taken out from military no doubt about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That was not actually the question that I put to you, and that is not what the report says. The question I put to you is whether you recall that by the 18th of August all check-points in the area of Knin are now manned by the Croatian police. I asked specifically about the police. Do you see -- do you see that, the second sentence there in the report. So, you see, it doesn't say that General Cermak took over all the check-points, and as I say, the question I have for you is: Do you recall on the ground that that is it what took place by the 18th of August, that the civilian Croatian police had taken control of all of the check-points in the area of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, no need, I take it, to draw your attention to the fact that the answer, although not to your question, was given and is, well, it's a rather sweeping statement. I don't know whether you want to explore whether there is any factual basis for that. I'm just drawing your attention to the fact that this is now evidence, not to say what weight to be given to it but --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can explore it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What evidence on the ground did you see to demonstrate the fact that the police were manning now running all of the check-points? Did you see uniformed members of the police by the 18th of August on check-points in and around Knin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you might have misunderstood what I said. Let me just check it exactly what point it was. It was about the role of Mr. Cermak. You see that the witness said after he had arrived, yes. "As soon as General Cermak arrived and took over command over the sector, so of this terrain, territory, that he -- so I do feel myself that he took over control and check-points from military not later than maybe." So this witness by these answers, by this answer suggests that it was all under Mr. Cermak's control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I was actually coming back to this issue later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you come to that fine, but the witness answered a question which was not put to him, but of course the answer is there on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, we'll address the issue immediately. I do want to come back to the position of Mr. Cermak. But can you tell the Judges who told you that General Cermak had taken over all of the check-points within the area the Knin? Who gave that you information?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: So generally we have differing sources of information to be able to analyse situation development on the ground. So from different source, reliable, unreliable, United Nations reliable sources, et cetera. So if we received such information that -- particularly about what you're just asking about, that means that United Nations Military Observers saw themselves these check-points and they reported that they saw it, or, in addition, we received information that there is change of -- and establishment of check-points on the main roads and they're manning and their timetable and et cetera. So then it is summarizing and then it is it put down in daily highlights.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I don't have a great deal of time and I wanted to put the question to you directly again and I will rephrase it. I'm right in saying that nobody specifically told you that General Cermak was in charge of all of the check-points around Knin, did they?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, I do not see here any mentioning in daily sitrep about General Cermak, so -- and that's why I just not to raise such questions to me repeatedly. I would just use then governmental authorities, because we're just returning back to specify. So if we see the fact and file it down, there is rotation, there are, you know, block roads and check-points established and that military handed over their control of the zone. And it is not the question, I mean, whether it is it direct, under the command of Mr. Cermak or through his deputies and those responsible for this one, it is like the same we have within the United Nations everywhere. So my point is that, yes, it was reported. It was seen by United Nations Military Observers that such rotations from military to structures in charge for the situation in the terrain took place and that was what an OPs officer put it down so to me it is very clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But, now, again, you're referring to the report itself which is speaking of the Croatian police taking over the check-points, aren't you? That's what you're referring to when you give that answer?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There's nothing in this document, is there, that suggests that General Cermak was ever in control of the check-points in the area of Knin, is there?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, you're agreeing with me?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you that in this particular sentence there is no name of General Cermak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can't tell the Court, can you, that anybody ever positively told you that General Cermak was in charge of the check-points in the area of Knin, can you?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could look at the last page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, nevertheless, I would like to understand exactly what the testimony of the witness in this respect is. In one of your earlier questions you suggested that these check-points, that the position of Mr. Cermak had to do something with that. Now, you also -- your testimony is that at a certain point these check-points were manned by the police. Did you consider Mr. Cermak to have any hierarchical position within the police which would make him such that the functioning of the check-points was in any way related to his position or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we do consider that, because, you know, all the protests and information sent about human rights violations filed and presented to General Cermak's office mentioned such cases, and we repeatedly received from him information that there was -- that he would take appropriate measures and all means available to ensure that the security and order on the roads, with the local population will be controlled and monitored and that was insurance given. And we see here clear evidence when General Cermak was in Knin in our location there, headquarters, in where he promised that he will provide and he will ensure it. So that's why I'm confident that if a person states that I'm in charge of this terrain, I do not think that I can blame, you know, chief of police of Knin, or whatever his name, I was asked just for what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we have to split up two periods. We're now talking about the period where the check-points were manned by the police, whereas at least this Chamber has received some evidence that at earlier stages there was a mixed composition of the -- of the crews, that is military and police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, for the two periods, say, I assumed on the basis that he responded to complaints we addressed to him that he must have had something to do with -- and he gave his commitments. So that is your position, on the basis of that you concluded that, as you said in one of your answers that: "I feel myself that he took over control and check-points from military not later than maybe three or four days after the end of Operation Storm." Now, when it was still -- these check-points were still of mixed composition, do you consider that the explanation that you just gave about involvement or -- is that for these early stages after he arrived or is it only after the police had taken over these check-points from the mixed -- mixed composition check-point teams?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If that were the question, I'm sorry, I just didn't properly just -- I got your idea, yes. Yes, we had, you know, gradual change of the composition of check-points, so initially for sure they were military. Then in some areas, well, specified areas let me say so, there were mixed check-points and they were reported by United Nations UNMOs about such mixed composition, particularly when you go out to the north and some more dangerous areas there. So it was gradually and the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you at that time, when they were still of mixed composition in some areas, did you also address Mr. Cermak and did you receive answers from Mr. Cermak at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During Operation Storm, I mean, all our addresses and discussions about new mandates and how we implemented it and what we found were reported and informed to Mr. Cermak office, whether they were on military mixed composition of check-points or whenever, because, you know, in headquarters and everywhere, we were presented that this is the focal points of Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you received on from the moment that you started addressing Mr. Cermak responses from him or through his office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes we got some and we already seen one of such report. And at least to the best of my knowledge, I do not recollect that we had ever addressed any just information or protest on a sector level to anyone but Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please go -- this is the last page of the report that we are just been looking at, Mr. Ermolaev, and you will see that there is a section there on restriction of movement. And you will see it is talking about "01 Sibenik team." So that is the UNMO team Sibenik; yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that a "yes"?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you will see there that, at 1815 hours, Bravo east of Drnis Croatian police. The Croatian police ignored the letter from General Cermak concerning freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Mm-hm, right. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you have previously -- you have previously given evidence, and it is in your statement, too, that it was your experience that on occasions General Cermak's authorisation to travel on roads was not accepted by the local authorities in the area who were controlling the check-point. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is a specific example of that, the Croatian police actually ignoring Mr. Cermak's authority?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of this particular example?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I was aware of everything, you know, on that days; so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were aware of this example?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: At that days, yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know why his authority was ignored on that particular day in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: You know, on 18th of August, I'm sorry, I was in Zadar, you know. I had my CTO, so I cannot just remember and just know what really happened there, because I was on my CTO, as I have already told.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was not at the mission. So I was, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to actually move now to another topic with you, and that is regarding General Cermak's authority within the region. I want to, first of all, read back to you part of your statement, and this is the first statement, Mr. Ermolaev. It's the page -- page 6, paragraph 3, where you state: "I assume that General Cermak purposely or not, but did not prevent the clearly seen by anyone gross human rights violations in the area of his command and control over the troops on the ground?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you a document which, I think, it needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The new procedure is, Mr. Cayley, you put the document to the witness, once the witness has answered questions about the witness; and the Prosecution will tell us whether there are any objections against it, and then it will be -- a number will be assigned to it and then we will decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have actually lost the transcript, Your Honour. For some reason, it is not -- it's back now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We do not assign numbers when the document is presented to a witness, but once the witness has answered questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. The document is, in fact, 2D02-0017.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ermolaev, what interests me in this document is not the content but it is an order from General Cermak, and you will see that it comes from the Ministry of Defence, main headquarters HV, garrison town Knin, and Mr. Cermak signs as the commander. Now, the question I have for you is this: Do you see what I have just read out, so that we're following each other?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah. I haven't read it yet, but I see it just in front of me, "I order," yeah?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. And you see in the first paragraph, at the top of the page, it has four lines. The last line reads "garrison town Knin"?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Right, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you see that Mr. Cermak at the bottom right-hand corner signs as the commander.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you were serving in Sector South, were you aware that that is what Mr. Cermak's official position was within Sector South, as the commander of the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to anyone about what official position Mr. Cermak occupied during this time?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: When we had, you know, our first meeting, and while presenting there and discussing situation in Sector South in the area of our responsibility, and particularly in Knin, my conclusions, my assessment, and understanding was that General Cermak was in charge of the whole territory; at least as I just remember it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That was your impression. Did General Cermak or anybody else ever tell you that he was this charge of the whole territory, as you put it? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. So, we saw this clearly in this film as well, at least as I got. It was a little bit quick. But, generally, everywhere and when we put protests about human rights --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you, because I need you to answer the specific question that I put to you, and the question is this: Did General Cermak or anyone else ever tell that he was in charge of the whole territory in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: It is a little bit, you know, strange question to me, because all activities and reports were sent to General Cermak; and he answered and he asked us to send him examples not only about the Knin garrison - let me finish - but about situation on the ground. So, alongside with that, I cannot confirm now exactly that, I mean, the position you mentioned. I started recollecting something about it. But at least as I'm confident, there was no one, another one, who would accept the reports that were prepared about the activities in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware, if at all, of the legal responsibilities of the garrison commander in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: So I know, as just turning back, all our requests to, you know, to prepare, for example, water supplies, to do something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to focus. Mr. Cayley, you have asked the witness whether he knew that the position Mr. Cermak held was that of garrison commander. He said he didn't know that. So why ask about specific functions of a garrison commander if the witness doesn't even know that that was the position of Mr. Cermak. Of course, the Chamber has received quite some evidence on that. I mean, to elicit from this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will move on Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We need an exhibit number for this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, any objection about the fish farm? That is what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D149 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One moment, please, Mr. President. Thank you. If we could please have P147, and, if, please, we could go --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to orientate yourself, Mr. Ermolaev, this is a report from the 11th of September of 1995. Were you back from leave then and back at work by that time?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yeah. I think I returned back after -- it was about a week only, so, I mean, that is 11 September.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please go to page five.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing that I may need some time to recollect, or maybe later, about when I departed, because then I departed, you know, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You departed in October; you recall that, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: In October?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you leave later than that; is it that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: I think that I arrived to the mission area on the 1st October 1994. So, according to rules, I was supposed to depart on the 1st of October after one year. I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you mentioned it in your statement, and we can certainly go back it that when you departed.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the page that interests me is page 5. It is 9730 and it's paragraph C, and if you could read that paragraph. Now, the part that interests me is what is stated about General Cermak, and you can see there that it states that: "His headquarters was in Knin and that he deals with non-operational matters." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And on non-operational matters, like the last order, getting fish farms working again; yes? I'll put a question to you: Do you understand the meaning of "non-operational"?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, in such particular context, I do not understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could it be that being non-operational is a senior military officer who it not involved in military operations? Would that be a fair explanation of what that means?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree that that that means that non-military activity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that would include, if one was not involved in military activity, it's also the case, isn't it, that that individual would not be in command of troops on the ground, would they?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: No. But it is clearly stated here that General Gotovina has his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's not the question that I put to you. What I'm saying is that if an individual was non-operational, logically that person would not have soldiers under their command in the field, would they?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV
utterances.text: Well, I would not like to discuss logic, so let me comment a bit about this summary of meetings. So, first of all, that information was received from senior Croatian liaison officer, and we received all information from all parties. And as a rule, such information is the information they, you know, mostly want us to receive. And, to such extent, I do not consider it is as a fact or just something telling to me that if some liaison officer told something to someone, this is not a fact and we just put it down; I mean, all such meetings with liaison officer. But I can assure you all such information we very critically considered what information we received from liaison officers of conflicting parties or any other sources which is not confirmed by United Nations Military Observer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt, Mr. Cayley. You're asking the witness now to interpret two words, and you are drawing all kind of -- or you're suggesting to the witness to draw all kind of logical conclusions from that: "Would it be logical that if you're ..."
